planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to deep shade; Oblongata Palm needs protection from direct sun and cold.

directions: Plant in shade to deep shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Oblongata Palm is an understory clumping or solitary palm from the rainforests of southern Mexico, including the Yucatan margins, through Honduras, bearing glossy, broad-leafleted pinnate fronds that reach 5-10 feet. It needs consistently bright shade, constant moisture, and protection from both direct sun and cold temperatures, making it a houseplant or protected courtyard specimen outside zones 10b-11. Its broad leaflets give it a bolder, more tropical look than some of the finer-textured Chamaedorea species already in cultivation.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into moist, well-drained soil in deep shade; Pacaya is often clump-planted in groups of several individuals for a fuller understory effect.

directions: Plant in deep shade in moist, well-drained soil; Pacaya is a solitary, slender-trunked feather palm ranging from Mexico through the Caribbean, including the Lesser Antilles and Trinidad, into South America, reaching 8-10 feet at maturity. It is somewhat more cold-tolerant than many Chamaedorea species, surviving briefly to about 30°F, and is a classic deep-shade rainforest-floor species often planted in clumps of several individuals for a fuller look. Give it consistent moisture and protection from direct sun, as with other understory palms.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into moist, well-drained soil in deep shade; Window Pane Palm is one of the most shade-tolerant ornamental palms available, suited to indoor or deeply shaded patio culture.

directions: Plant in deep shade in moist, well-drained soil; Window Pane Palm is a dwarf clustering palm reaching only 3-5 feet, native to the rainforest understory of Mexico, Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, and Panama. It is named for distinctive translucent perforations, or 'windows,' in its leaflets, an unusual and attractive trait among palms. It is one of the most shade-tolerant ornamental palms available, popular as an indoor houseplant or deeply shaded patio specimen where almost no other palm would survive.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich soil in part shade to shade; Powdery Spiral Ginger is a true forest-floor understory species.

directions: Plant in part shade to shade in moist, humus-rich soil; Powdery Spiral Ginger ranges from Mexico through Central America to Caribbean-adjacent lowlands, bearing blue-green leaves with striking purple undersides on stems reaching 3-6 feet, with red bracts and yellow flowers. It is a true forest-floor understory species, more shade-tolerant than many of the sun-loving ornamental gingers already in cultivation. Note that common-name mislabeling across Costus species is frequent in the nursery trade, so verify the species tag before purchase.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in part shade to full sun; Small-Leaf Clusia is commonly clipped as a hedge but reaches 20 feet or more unclipped.

directions: Plant in part shade to full sun in well-drained soil; Small-Leaf Clusia is a Caribbean-native shrub or small tree with thick, glossy leaves, distinct from the already-grown autograph tree (Clusia rosea) in its smaller leaf scale and more flexible light tolerance. It is extensively used across South Florida as a hedge, typically kept at 4-8 feet with regular clipping, though it will reach 20 feet or more if left unpruned. It is salt- and drought-tolerant once established, a versatile landscape choice for both sunny and shaded sites in zones 10b-11.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in part shade; this Caribbean-island relative of the already-present Florida Keys joewood is a genuine specialty-nursery find.

directions: Plant in part shade in well-drained soil; this Caribbean-island joewood is native to Hispaniola, Puerto Rico, and the Lesser Antilles, distinct from the already-grown Florida Keys endemic Jacquinia keyensis. It grows as a shrub to small tree 6-15 feet tall, with narrow leathery leaves, fragrant flowers, and orange fruit, occupying the understory margin of dry coastal forest in its native range. It is drought-tolerant once established and is a genuine specialty-nursery find, described by at least one source as hard-to-find in cultivation.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained, rocky soil in part shade; Caribbean Princewood is drought-tolerant once established, suiting a Florida Keys or Caribbean-style hammock planting.

directions: Plant in part shade in well-drained, rocky soil; Caribbean Princewood is a shrub or small tree reaching 20-30 feet, native to Florida Keys hammocks, the Yucatan Peninsula, and the wider Caribbean dry and rocky forest understory and edge. Large, fragrant white tubular flowers make it a worthwhile addition to a native hammock or dry-forest-themed planting. It is drought-tolerant once established, suited to the same understory and forest-edge conditions as the already-present Bourreria ovata and Jacquinia keyensis.
sources: Key West Tropical Forest & Botanical Garden

planting.note: Plant container-grown seedlings in spring into moist, well-drained soil in shade; Manac Palm spends many years as a shaded understory juvenile before reaching its full mature height.

directions: Plant seedlings in shade in moist, well-drained soil; Manac Palm is a riparian moist-forest palm endemic to Puerto Rico, with a sister species on Hispaniola and Cuba, and spends many years as a shaded understory juvenile before eventually reaching 30-40 feet as a mature feather palm. It is genuinely rare in cultivation, with supply limited to specialty palm seed and seedling vendors rather than general retail, so confirm current stock before planning a planting around it. Give young plants consistent moisture and bright shade, mimicking the streamside forest habitat it occupies naturally.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in part shade; Bahama Strongback tolerates the filtered light typical of a hammock sub-canopy position.

directions: Plant in part shade in well-drained soil; Bahama Strongback is a weeping evergreen tree reaching 15-25 feet, native to Florida Keys hammocks and the wider Caribbean including the Bahamas and Cuba. It bears fragrant white flowers nearly year-round, making it a strong pollinator plant distinct from the already-present Bourreria ovata. It tolerates the filtered light of a hammock sub-canopy position well, making it a good choice for the understory tier of a native tropical hammock planting rather than full open sun.
